OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Honourable Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shri Arangil Sreedharan, a former Member of this House, on the 
13th December, 2001, at the age of 78. 
Born at Badagara, Kerala, in March, 1923, Shri Sreedharan had his education at 
Badagara, Mangalore, Calicut and Vellore. A dedicated political and social worker, 
Shri Sreedharan'took an active part in the "Quit India Movement" in 1942. He was 
also associated with various trade unions and championed the cause of the weaker 
sections of the society. He was imprisoned on several occasions in connection 
with the agitation of farmers and workers. Shri Sreedharan was the Chairman 
of the Indian Socialist Party from 1961 to 1971. 
Shri Sreedharan started his legislative career as a Member of the Fourth Lok 
Sabha. He represented the State of Kerala in this House from July, 1988 to July, 
1994. He also served as the Minister of State of Commerce from April, 1990 to 
November, 1990. 
In the passing away of Shri Sreedharan the country has lost a freedom 
fighter, an active social worker and a veteran parliamentarian. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Arangil Sreedharan. 
I also wish to place on record the sacr ifice of Shri Matbar Singh, Security 
Assistant of Watch and Ward Service, Rajya Sabha Secretariat, who was 
injured in the terrorists' attack on Parliament on the 13th December, 2001 and 
succumbed to his injuries on the 16th December, 2001. 
Shri Matbar Singh showed an exemplary courage and devotion to duty by 
closing the building Gate No. 11, even though hit by bullets 
1 

RAJYA SABHA       [18 December, 2001] 
in the terrorists' shoot-out thereby averting an unimaginable disaster. His 
selfless and courageous deed has thus set an example for others to emulate 
and all of us feel proud. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Matbar Singh. 
I request Members to rise in their pl aces and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General w ill convey to the members of the 
bereaved families our sense of profound sorrow and deep sympathy.

LPG dealership in North Bengal 
* 386. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACH ARJEE. Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that allotments of LPG dealership in North Bengal 
towns like Falakata and Mathabhanga were done by the Oil Selection Board 
in an arbitrary manner; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the unemployed women graduates 
belonging to SC community were not considered for allotment and if so, the 
reasons therefor; and 
(c) whether firm allotments have since been made Jor LPG 
dealership in Falakata and Mathabhanga and if not, by when the 
same is likely to be made? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (c) The Government have issued guidelines to provide for 
transparent, uniform and fair procedure for selection of suitable candidates as 
retail outlet dealers, LPG distribu tors and SKO-LDO dealers. These 
guidelines, infer alia, include eligibility criteria, reservation for different 
categories, procedure for invitation of applications, norms for evaluation of 
candidates, time-frame for selection, the Grievance Redressal System, etc. 
The action with regard to complain ts received against the empanelled 
candidates and the selection process is taken as per the Grievance Redressal 
System laid down in the guidelines. 
The   guidelines   for  selection  provide  for  25%   reservation   for 
7 

RAJYA SABHA      [18 December, 2001] 
Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes fo r dealerships/distributorships. The 
guidelines also provide for 33% rese rvation for women in each category 
including Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes. 
One Letter of Intent (LOI) has been issued by Bharat Petroleum 
Corporation Limited (BPCL) for a LPG distributorship on 10.8.2001 in 
Falakata and one LOI has been issued by Indian Oil Corporation Limited 
(IOCL) for LPG distributorship on 25.7.2001 in Mathabhanga in West 
Bengal.

Performance of LIC 
*388. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the overall performance of LIC in the last few years have 
deteriorated; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether NPAs have been mounting and if so, the steps taken to 
expedite recovery of outstanding loan which is slow; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government to improve the performance and 
financial health of LIC in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) No, Sir. The overall performance 
of Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) has improved during the last few years. 
Details regarding growth in new business (First Premium Income) of LIC from 
1998 to 2W)1 are given in the Statement (See below). 
11 

RAJYA SABHA      [18 December, 2001] 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. LIC has intimated that the NPAs of the Corporation have 
declined in the last few years. As regards recovery of outstanding loans, constant 
efforts are made by the Corporation to recover the outstanding dues by following 
up with the defaulting corporate entities, concerned State agencies/Government, 
etc. A separate monitoring cell has been set up to monitor such recoveries. The 
action taken includes restructuring of liabilities in consultation with other financial 
institutions, taking up the matter with Debenture Trustees, identification of wilful 
defaulters as per RBI guidelines, instituting legal proceedings and linking release of 
fresh loans with clearance of outstanding loans. The Corporation also attends 
the Heads of Institutions Meetings (HIM) wherein relief packages for companies 
are discussed and implemented in deserving cases. Further, Government has 
delegated functional autonomy to LIC and experts have been inducted from various 
fields on the Board of the Corporation.

Toning up of corporate governance 
2915. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any step to tone up Corporate 
Governance; 
(b) whether inview of the market manipulations in recent past it has 
become imperative to bring about n ecessary changes for reforming the 
systems of Corporate Governance; and 
(c) what steps Government contemplates to take in near future in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SING H): (a) to (c) Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (SEBI) set up a Committee on Corporate 
Governance on May 7, 1999 to promote and raise the standards of Corporate 
Governance. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, SEBI 
directed stock exchanges to amend their 
56 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
listing agreements to implement the mandatory recommendations of the 
Committee. SEBI has made some of the best practices of corporate 
governance mandatory, through a phased programme. The board of directors 
of a company shall have an optimum  combination of executive and nog-
executive directors with not less than 50% of the boards consisting of non-
executive directors. A qualified and independent audit committee is required 
to be set up, which will meet at least thrice a year. The annual reports of 
companies are required to have a separate section on corporate governance. 
The new clause in the listing agreement also lays down board procedures 
including the frequency of board meetings. Further, a director shall not be a 
member in more than 10 committees or act as Chairman of more than five 
committees across all companies in which he is a Director. Shareholders are 
to be provided information in case of appointment of a new Director or re-
appointment of a Director. A board committee is to be formed to look into 
redressal of shareholder and investor complaints. The Government has also 
instituted a National Award for Excellence in Corporate Governance.

the year 1999-2000. However, this decline is mainly due to increase in 
production and area under cultivation of areca nut. the Government has taken

further expansion in area under the crop, as it has no alternative use other 
than the masticatory purpose. The expert Committee has also recommended 
steps to increase the productivity so as to increase the income from unit area 
through crop diversification in the existing arecanut plantations and the need

2922. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH): (a ) to (c) It has been the 
constant endeavour of the Government  to safeguard the interest of the 
employees of Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs), who opt out on 
Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) or become redundant due to 
restructuring of the enterprises. A modified VRS for the employees of CPSUs 
has been introduced vide Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) 
notification dated 5.5.2000. In order to further safeguard the interest of the 
workers of sick and loss making PSUs, particularly those where wage 
revision has not been effected after 1.1.1987 or 1.1.1992, as the case may be, 
the compensation package has been enhanced by 100% and 50% 
respectively. The compensation of retr enched employees is governed under 
the Industrial Dispute Act, further liberalization of whose provisions are 
being examined by the Ministry of Labour. 
Further, in pursuance of the Industrial Policy of the Government, to 
provide a safety net to the employees of the organized sector, a National 
Renewal Fund (NRF) was set up by the Government in February, 1992.

towards voluntary retirement of employees of CPSUs as also for 
rehabilitation of the employees of the organized

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA

adminsterd the scheme till 31.3.2001.

scheme for Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment of rationalised employees 
of Central PSUs with an objective to reorient the rationalised employees of 
CPSUs through short duration training programmes to encourage them to avail of 
opportunities of self employment after their separation from the PSEs due to VRS 
or retrenchement due to closure of the enterprise. In order to have wide coverage of 
the scheme and its proper implementation at the national level, nodal agencies have 
been selected from different States to cater to the needs of the rationalised 
employees of the CPSUs. The training programme has already started.

† 2935. SHRI KHAN GHUFRAN ZAHIDI: Will the Minister of FINANCE

(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item captioned, 
"America per Aatankwadi Hamlay Nay Vikassheel Deshon Main Gareebee

† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
77 

RAJYA SABHA       [18 December, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Yes sir. The news item refers to the 
observations made by the Finance Ministers at the Development Committee 
Meeting of the Boards of Governors of the World Bank and the International 
Monetary Fund held in Ottawa on November 18, 2001 under the 
chairmanship of the Finance Minister of India (Shri Yashwant Sinha). The 
Ministers reviewed the impact of the September 11, terrorist attacks and their 
aftermath on developing countries. They recognized that poverty in many 
developing countries was likely to worsen as these events have deepened the 
pre-existing global economic slowdown, which had already led to weaker 
exports and commodity prices, and have other more specific impacts; e.g., 
increased refugee movements within co untries and across borders; reduced 
private investment flows due to increased risk aversion in financial markets; 
reduced tourism revenues; and increased trade transaction costs. 
(b) and (c) The longer term economic impact of the terrorist attack in USA 
and the subsequent war in Afghanistan on the Indian economy will depend 
upon the duration and intensity of the war and its impact on global demand 
and trade. There has been some effect  of the war on Indian exports, stock 
markets, tourism, heightened risk aversion of foreign investors and the 
foreign exchange market. However, Indi a's share in international trade and 
finance is marginal and the Government has adopted credible economic 
reforms with a focus on generation of employment and reduction of poverty. 
Mereover, in its mid-term review of the monetary and credit policy for the 
year 2001-02, announced in October 2001, the Reserve Bank of India has 
projected 5-6 per cent growth for the Indian economy for the year 2001-2002.

2953. SHRI NANA DESH MUKH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Kisan Credit Cards would be associated with crop and personal 
insurance which in case of permanent disability would enable him to get Rs. 
24,000/- and in case of death his heir would get Rs. 50,000/- which in the present 
days of inflation is too less amount; 
(b) whether the crop insurance benefit is being implemented taking crops as a 
unit for famine or other natural calamity; and 
91 

RAJYA SABHA      [18 December, 2001] 
(c) if so, what steps are being taken to Government to give the crop 
insurance benefits on individual benefits and increase the quantum of 
personal insurance? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Under the Kisan Credit card (KCC) Scheme, 
the farmers avail crop loans to meet th eir production and contingency needs. 
Under National Agricultural insurance Scheme (NAIS), the fanners availing loans 
through Kisan Credit Cards for raising notified crops, within the purview of the 
provisions of the Scheme, are covered for crop losses only. The Scheme of 
Personal Accident Policy for KCC holders, launched on 10.10.2001, provides 
personal accident insurance to cover them against accidental death or 
permanent total disability for a sum insured of Rs. 50,000/- while for permanent 
partial disability, the compensation is Rs. 25,000/-. The premium payable for 
one year policy is Rs. IV- per person to be shared by the KCC holder and the 
issuing bank in the ratio of 2:1. The coverage is considered adequate at the 
existing level of premium. 
(b) NAIS operates on the basis of 'Area Approach' i.e. defined areas for each 
notified crop for widespread calamities and on an 'individual basis' in limited areas 
for localised calamities, such as, hailstorm, landslide, cyclone and floods, on an 
experimental basis. The defined area (i.e. unit of insurance) may be Gram 
panchayat, Mandal, Hobli, Circle, Phirka, Block, Taluka, etc., as decided by the 
State Government/Union Territory but  each participating State/ Union 
Territory is requird to leach the level of Gram Panchayat within a period of 3 
years. 
(c) There is no proposal under consideration of the Government to implement 
the Crop Insurance on an individual basis or increasing the quantum of 
personal insurance.

the State of Gujarat due to attempted pilferage by some miscreants. The

Decline in production capacity of Mumbai High 
3005. SHRI NANA DE SHMUKH: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Mumbai High which commenced production of 
oil in 1976 did produce 4 lakh barrels of oil per day between 1985 and 1989; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the production has declined to 2.2 lakh 
barrels and the production of gas has also come down; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to boost the production of both these items 
again? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) to (c) The 
Mumbai High field of Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. (ONGC) started 
production in 1976 and entered in the declining phase of production from 1990-91, 
which is a natural phenomenon for any aging field, thus, while the Mumbai 
High field reached its peak production of 4 lakh barrels of oil per day during the 
period 1985-89, the average production has declined gradually to about 2.20 lakh 
barrels per day of oil in November 2001. The gas production has also come down 
to 14.17 million standard cubic metres per day (MMSCMD) in November 2001 
from the peak level of 26.83 MMSCMD. 
(d) In order to improve the recovery of oil and gas from the Mumbai High 
(M.H.) field, ONGC has taken up the redevelopment of M.H. North and M.H. 
South Fields, which envisages an incremental production of about 75 million 
metric tonnes of oil and oil equivalent of gas over a 30 years time-frame.

† 3034. SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
    Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of States identified by Government who suffer excess of 
water or lay behind for want of water;

under-way for the supply thereof; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(Ms. BUOY A CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Availability of water in the 
country varies both temporally as well as spatially. As a result, a number of areas 
receive excessive rainfall and get flooded while other areas face drought like 
situation due to scarcity of the rainfall. Rashtriya barh Ayog (1988) assessed 
that about 34 million hectares of area in the country is prone to floods. The 
state wise details are given in the Statement I (See below). 
At the same time, as per the basinwise assessement made by Central Water 
Commission (1993), Sabarmati, Pennar, Cauvary, Tapi and Mahi basins, in additon 
to areas in Rajasthan, Kutch and Saur ashtra region, have per capita water 
availability below 1000 cubic metre per year, which according to certain International 
organizations represents a scarcity condition. The names of basins covering 
different states and the per capita water availability therein is given in the 
Statement II (see below) 
(c) and (d) Requirement of water is closely related to population, demand for 
food, production of ind jstrial items, production of energy and preserving ecology. 
The availability of water for use for diverse purposes has increased over the Plan 
periods by creation of the live storage capacity of 177 (BCM) by construction of 
large dams upto 1995. An additional live storage capacity of 75 BCM will be 
created on completion of dams, which are under various statges of 
construction. Proposals to take up additional dams to create a live storage   
capacity   of   132   BCM   are    also   under   formulation/

3035. SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to a reported 
statement of Union Minister of State for Communications published in a 
Bengali Daily from Kolkata "Sambad pratidin" on 28th October, 
185 

RAJYA SABHA      [18 December, 2001] 
2001 to the effect that the agreem ent between India and Bangladesh to 
distribute Ganga Water between these two countries signed in 1997 should be 
reviewed;

any formal demand for the review of the Ganga Water agreement? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRYF OF WATER 
RESOURCES (MS. BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Treaty between India and Bangladesh on sharing of Ganga 
waters at Farakka during lean period (January to May) was signed on 12th 
December, 1996. The Treaty itself has a provision for review by the two 
Governments at five years interval or earlier, as required by either party and 
needed adjustment, based on principles of equity, fairness and no harm to 
either party made thereto if necessary. The Government of Bangladesh has 
not so far made any formal demand for a review.

(c) Contents of the said^aragraph is considered objectionable and likely to

Statement 
The Varna System 
Religion influenced the formation of so cial classes in India in a peculiar 
way. In other ancient societies the dutie s and functions of social classes were 
fixed by law which was largely enforced by the state. But in India Varna laws 
enjoyed the sanction of both the state and   religion.   The   functions  of  
priests,  warriors,   peasants  and 
200 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
labourers were defined in law and supposed to have been laid down by divine 
agencies. Those who departed from their functions and were found guilty of 
offences were subjected to secular punishments. They had also to perform rituals 
and penances, all differing according to the Varna. Each Varna was given not 
only a social but also a ritualistic recognition. In course of time Varnas or social 
classes and jatis or castes were made hereditary by law and religion. All this was 
done to ensure that vaishyas produce and pay taxes and shudras serve as labourers 
so that brahmanas act as priests and kshatriyas as rulers. Based on the division of 
labour and specialization of occupations, the peculiar institution of the caste system 
certainly helped the growth of society and economy at the initial stage. The 
Varna system contributed to the development of the state. The producing and 
labouring classes were disarmed, and gradually each caste was pitted against the 
other in such a manner that the oppressed ones could not combine against the 
privileged classes. 
The need of carrying out their respective functions was so strongly ingrained in 
the minds of the various classes that ordinarily they would never think of 
deviating from their dharma. The Bhagavadgita taught that people should lay down 
their lives in defence of their own dharma rather than adopt the dharma of others, 
which would prove dangerous. The lower orders worked hard in the firm belief that 
they would deserve a better life in the next world or birth. This belief lessened 
the intensity and frequency of tensions and conflicts between those who actually 
produced and those who lived off these producers as princes, priests, officials, 
soldiers and big merchants. Hence the necessity for exercising coercion against the 
lower orders was not so strong in "Ancient India". What was done by slaves and 
other producing sections in Greece and Rome under the threat of whip was done by 
the vaishyas and shudra as out of conviction formed through brahmanical 
indoctrinations and the Varna system.

Research benefits to farmers 
2733. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: WU1 the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:     
(a) whether it is a fact that the agriculture research and education 
in the country is not in a position to impart research benefits to 
farmers, due to lack of financial support; 
(b) if so, what was the demand for agriculture research and 
education during the Ninth Five Year Plan; 
(c) whether the demand had been met; if not, the reasons therefor; 
and 
(d) what steps Government propose to take to provide the 
required/demanded amount? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Though there is a paucity of 
funds, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) is imparting 
research benefits to farmers. The Council have established Krishi Yigyan 
Kendras (KVKs) in various parts of th e Country, the activities of which are 
on-farm testing to identify the location specificity of technology in various 
farming systems, frontline demonstration to establish the production 
potentiality on farmers' field, skill training of farmers to update their 
knowledge in modern agricultural technology, and training of extension 
personnel to orient them in the frontier areas of technology development. 
During the year 2000-01 a total of 17 thousand training courses covering 4.18 
lakhs farmers and rural youths have been 
216 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
trained by these KVKs including 1.5 th ousand training courses covering 35 
thousand extension personnel. In order to speed-up process of dissemination of 
agricultural technology, during the year 2000-01, the KVKs organised various 
extension activities including kisan melas (246), field days (1215), kisan 
goshties (1043), films shows (761), exhibition (170), newspaper coverages (2192) 
and other activities (3061) were undertaken by KVKs. Besides, conducting 
about 22895 frontline demonstration to establish the production potentials of the 
newly released production technologies on the farmers plots, a large number of 
on farm trials were undertaken to identify the location specificity of technology 
under various farming systems. However, in these days of international 
competition on science and technology based research, particularly bio-
technology, the need is of a much higher order. If this is made available the 
servicing of the farmers can be tremendously improved. 
(b) The Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE) had 
formulated its need based projections during IX Plan in accordance of 1% of 
Agricultural Gross Domestic Product as also recommended by IX Plan Working 
Group and Parliamentary Standing Committee on Agriculture (PSCA), which 
was at Rs. 7800 crore + Rs. 500 crore as Catch UP Grant meant for renovation and 
modernization of old infrastructure, equipments and other research facilities of the 
National Agricultural Research. System. In this way a total of Rs. 8300 crore was 
demanded by DARE/ICAR in the IX Plan. 
(c) During Ninth Plan Period, the Planning Commission had allocated an 
amount of Rs. 3376.95 crore including Rs. 400 crore as Catch UP Grant in respect 
of DARE/ICAR. However the same has now been curtailed to Rs. 2514.17 
crore. 
(d) Since the IX Plan allocation has been of a much lower order than the 
need, the capacity of ICAR for absorbing funds has also become proportionately 
limited by the end of the IX pian period. Therefore, for the X Plan period the 
DARE/ICAR's requirement has been projected Rs. 15000 crore + Rs. 1000 
crore as Catch up Grant. If an allocation of this order is received, it is expect* d 
that the 
217 

RAJYA SABHA      [18 December, 2001] 
DARE/ICAR will be able to absorb the projected funds and after this period, 
will develop the capacity to absorb the entire allocation of 1% of 
Agricultural GDP. The Department is continuously pursuing the matter with 
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance to meet the projected 
requirement of funds during the balance period of Ninth Plan and the Tenth 
Plan.

Statement I 
Macro Management of Agriculture 'Supplementation/Complementation of 
States' Efforts through Work Plan' 
Objective: Macro Management scheme will  aim  at  all  round 
development   in   agriculture   through   Work   Plans 
prepared by State. These include. 
• Reflection   of  local   needs/crop/regions  specific/ 
priorities etc. 
• Providing flexibility and autonomy to States; 
• Optimum utilization of scarce financial resource; 
• Maximisation of returns; 
• Removal of regional imbalances. 
Salient features: It has been decided to move away from schematic approach 
to Macro management mode by integrating 27 Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes (a list is annexed). The previous 
pattern of rigid uniformly structured Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes, permitting little or no flexibility, which resulted in 
large unutilised balances with states has been dispensed 
with. Integration of Centrally Sponsored Schemes under 
Macro management approach will enhance the productivity 
of support programmes and accord greater flexibility to 
State Governments to develop and pursue activities on the 
basis of regional priorities.  It is, 
230 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
thus, a major step towards ach ieving decentralization in 
pursuance of restoring primacy  of States in agricultural 
development planning. The Central Government will 
supplement/complement the State Government's efforts 
through regionally differentiated Work Plans comprising 
crop/area/ target group specific interventions, formulated in 
an interactive mode and implemented in spirit of 
partnership with the States. 
Pattern of The outlay of the Work Plan would be shared by 
assistance: the Centre and the States in the ratio of 90:10. In the 
case of North-Eastern States, however, the entire 
expenditure will be borne by the Government of India. 
Central assistance for Work Plans will be in the ratio of 80 
by grants and 20% by loans.

Boards; Oilseeds production programme;

(a) These schemes aim to increase the production and productivity of the 
respective crops through Supply of quality planting material of improved 
varieties and making available technical know-how to growers through 
trainings and demonstrations. The scheme on State

These Schemes, except the scheme on Oilseeds Production Programme, 
have now been subsumed, since October, 2000, in the scheme on macro 
management of agriculture-Supplementation/ complementation of States' efforts 
through work plans. Under these schemes States have greater flexibility to prioritise

Ban on fishing in Arabian Sea 
2748. SHRI  A.  VIJAYA RAG HAVAN:  Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to stop fishing of certain fish 
varieties like shark, in the Arabian Sea; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government would consider to ban fishing of certain varieties 
of fish from our sea; and 
247 

RAJYA SABHA      [18 December, 2001] 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) Government of India, 
Ministry of Environment and Forests (MOEF) had issued a notification in July, 
2001 imposing ban on hunting of sharks and rays considering the fact that they have 
become rare and endangered due to over-exploitation to meet the increased 
international demand for their fins, meat, etc. This decision is reported to 
have been taken based on a scientific publication of Central Marine Fisheries 
Research Institute (CMFRI), Cochin. 
A large number of representations from various quarters were received 
asserting that the aforesaid ban would adversely affect the livelihood opportunities of 
large number of fishermen. A meeting was convened by MOEF recently to discuss 
the issue with the experts and scientists of various institutes in the country. Based 
on the views expressed in this meeting it was decided to give a three years research 
project on the issue to CMFRI and Zoological Survey of India to assess 
population status of individual species and quantum harvested annually. In the 
interim period the MOEF have decided to restrict the ban to ten shark species that 
are considered critically endangered and vulnerable by the International Union 
for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

† 2752. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
SHRI RAJIV RAN J AN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:

cultivated land holding of farmers in the country during the last many years; 
(b) if so, the average size of the cultivat ed land-holding in the country at 
present; 
(c) whether it is a fact that cultivation in this size of a holding has become 
economically unviable; and

of factors including agro-climatic, level of use of agricultural input,

skill of the farmer. No conclusive evidence is available regarding 
relationship between size of the holding and its economic viability.

Funding Central Schemes of Agricultural Development 
2765. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the salient features of the Centrally sponsored schemes of National-
Pulses Development Programme; Oil Palm Development Programme; 
Accelerated Maize Development Programme; Timely Reporting of Estimates 
of Area and Production of Principal Crops and Establishment on an Agency 
for Reporting of Agricultural Statistics (EARAS); 
(b) what are the criteria for allocating funds under each scheme to States 
and the corresponding Central share; whether these funds would be given to 
States as 100 per cent grant or whether it would follow the usual 70/30 
(loan/grant) formula for Plan Assistance; and 
(c) what are the State-wise details of proposals received, funds released 
and utilized during the last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) The Technology Mission 
on Oilseeds & Pulses has been implementing the Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes of National Pulses Develo pment Project (NPDP), Oil Palm 
Development Programme (OPDP) and Accelerated Maize Development 
Programme (AMDP). The salient features  of these schemes are that these 
schemes are Centrally Sponsored schemes being implemented on the sharing 
pattern of 75:25 between Government of India and the State Governments. 
Under these schemes, assistance is pr ovided to the farmers for different 
components through State Govts, for increasing the production of pulses, oil 
palm and maize in order to increase production of pulses, maize & edible 
oils. 
As regards, timely reporting of estimates of area and production of principal 
crops, a scheme for Timely Reporting System (TRS) is funded by the Govt, 
of India which takes care of sampling design of TRS for priority data 
collection based on prevalent land record 
275 

RAJYA SABHA      [18 December, 2001] 
system and timely completion of consolidation at district and thereafter a 
state level. Under the Establishment of an Agency for Reporting of 
Agricultural Statistics (EARAS) the scheme provides for setting up of a 
whole time agency to cover a sample of 20% of villages every year to 
generate basic land use statistics. The focus of EARAS is primary data 
collection and its supervision. 
(b) The criteria for allocating the funds under these schemes to 
States and the corresponding central share is based on their potential, 
past performance with regard to the production achievements and the 
expenditure incurred under different schemes. The funds are given as 
a grants-in-aid to the States on the sharing pattern of 75:25 under the 
scheme of NPDP, OPDP & AMDP an d there is no loan component 
under these schemes. However in case of TRS and EARAS, 100% 
grant is given to the States on 50:50 sharing basis between the 
Central Govt, and the State Govt, without any loan component. 
(c) The details of the fund alloca tion and release st ate-wise during 
the last 3 years are given in Annexure for NPDP, OPDP, AMDP, 
TRS & EARAS. [See Appendix 194, Annexure No. 25]

wildlife offenders.

lend a helping hand to field formations for curbing poaching and 
illegal trade in wildlife.

under the chairmanship of Secr etary (Environment and Forests),

Centrally sponsored educational schemes 
2810. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the salient features of the centrally sponsored schemes 
of Joint GOI-Un Programme for Primary Education; 
Sarvasiksha Abhiyan; National Programme for Women's 
Education; Literacy Campaign; Operation Restoration support 
to NGOs in the field of Adult Education (earlier Shramic 
Vidyapeeth); Counting Education for New Literates; Culture 
Exchange Programme; 
(b) what are the criteria fo r allocating funds under each 
scheme    to    States    and    the    corresponding    Central    share; 
320 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
whether these funds are given to States as 100 percent grant or the usual 
70/30 (loan/grant) formula is followed for Plan assistance; and 
(c) the details of proposals received, funds released and utilization for last 
three years. State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. (S HRIMATI) RITA VERM A): (a) 
The salient features of various centrally sponsored schemes referred to in the 
Question are as follows:— 
1. Janshala (Joint GOI-UN Programme): It is a community-based primary 
education programme with the objective of making primary education more 
accessible and effective, especially for girls and children of deprived 
communities, marginalised groups, SC/ST/ minorities, working children and 
children with special needs. The programme is a collaborative effort of the 
Government of India and five UN agencies viz. UNDP, UNICEF, UNESCO 
ILO and UNFPA to provide programme support to the ongoing efforts 
towards achieving Universalisation of Elementary Education. The programme 
presently covers 139 blocks and 10 cities in 31 districts spread over 9 States i.e. 
Andhra Pradesh, Chattis garh, Jharkhand, Karnat aka, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Orissa Rajasthan and U ttar Pradesh. The UN agencies have 
committed a contribution of US$ 20 million as a grant for this programme. 
2. Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA): It is a newly launched scheme with a 
holistic and integrated approach to acheive the objective of Universalisation of 
Elementary Education. The programme aims to provide useful and quality 
elementary education of 8 years to a ll children in the 6—14 age group by 
2010. The programme will cover all the districts in the country. The 
expenditure on the programme will be shared between Centre & States in the 
ratio 85:15 in the 9th Plan, 75:25 in the 10th Plan and 50:50 in the 11th Plan 
and in the subsequent Plan periods. 
321 

RAJYA SABHA       [18 December, 2001] 
3. National Programme for Women's Education: At present no such scheme is 
under operation. 
4. Literacy Campaigns and Operation Restoration: The Total Literacy 
Companies (TLC) is the principal strategy of the National Literacy Mission 
for eradication of illiteracy. Besides imparting functional literacy, it also 
include interventions for encreasing enrolement and retention of children in 
schools, immunisation, propagation of small family norms, promotion of 
maternity and child care, women's equally and empowerment, peace and 
communal harmony etc. On conclusion of TLC, Post Literacy Programme 
(PLP) is taken up for consolidation of lit eracy skills and integration of skill 
development programmes. Out of 598 districts in the country, 574 districts 
are covered under Adult Education programmes. The funding pattern is ratio 
of 2:1 and 4:1 between Centre and State Governments for normal and tribal 
districts respectively. 
5. Continuing Education: The scheme aims at providing further learning 
opportunities to neo-Literatcs by setting up Continuing Education Cetnres, to 
serve population of 2000-2500 by providing facilities of library, reading 
room, learning centre etc. The Central Government provides 100% funding 
for the first three years which is to be  shared between the Central and State 
Governments equally during the next two years. The scheme has been 
sanctioned to 112 districts in 18 States and Union Territories. Recurring 
assistance is provided to the Nodal and Continuing Education Centre @ Rs. 
45,000/- and 25,000/- per year respectively. A non-recurring assistance is also 
provided on the same scale once in five years. 
6. Jan Shikshan Sansthan (formerly known as Shramik Vidyapceth): The 
scheme aims to provide polyvalent or multi-faceted adult education 
programme by improving the vocational skills and quality of life of its 
beneficiaries, which are mostly nco-litcratcs, semi-literates and non-Literates. 
It concentrates on the socio-economically backward and educationally dis-
advantaged groups of urban/rural population, such as neo- litcrates, semi-
literates, SCs, STs, women and girls slum dwellers, migrant workers, etc. 
7. Culture Exchange Programme: Ministry of Culture is the nodal 
322 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
agency for formulation of Cultural Exchange Programmes and monitoring 
their implementation. Cultural Exchange Programmes incorporate specific 
provisions for exchanges such as visits of professors, experts, scholars, 
artists, writers, performing troupes sports teams, exhibitions, youth and 
children's groups, radio and TV programmes, awards of scholarships, training 
in specialised fields, institutional cooperation and participation in 
international, fairs, exhibitions, festivals etc. They also include items for 
establishment of institutional links, especially between universities and other 
institutions of higher education and re search. No State-wise releases have 
been made by this Department under these programmes. 
(b) and (c) The entire Central share for the above schemes is released as 
grant. Funds are released  to the concerned States/State Implementation 
Societies as per the funding pattern of various schemes, progress of 
expenditure, availability of unspent ba lances etc. In the case of Janshala 
(Joint GOI-UN Programme), funds we re released by the concerned UN 
agencies directly to the project States upto March, 2001 and therefore figures 
of expenditure are reported. In the case of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), 
since the programme was launched during the last financial year only, 
figures of utilisation of funds are yet to become available. In the case of 
schemes for Adult Education, unutilised funds during the year are allowed to 
be carried over to the next financial year. The information relating to funds 
sanctioned/expenditure on the above lines is given in the statement.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS

52,663,000 (Rs. 106 crore

approx.) The landed cost of these coaches is Rs. 159 crore (approx.). 
(b) Integral Coach Factory, Chennai and other Indian coach factories have 
so far been manufacturing coaches to the technology imported in the 1950s. 
Though, this technology has been progressively improved to higher speeds 
and better riding characteristics, it has been streched to its limits. As a result, 
the existing coaches have become very maintenace intensive. For any further 
increase in the speed of trains and to run longer trains with improved safety a 
quantum upgradation in technology of coaches was necessary. Indian Railways 
therefore, entered into a transfer of technology cont ract alongwith supply of

of coachs are being developed at Rail Coach Factory, Kapurthala and actual

lock centre buffer coupler. Such couplers will enable running of longer trains

minimise if not eliminate altogether loss of life and or injury to passengers 
during serious accident. These couplers  had been inducted for the first time 
for passenger coaches in the country. Some teething problems arose after a 
few weeks of running. The LHB design coaches running in Delhi-Lucknow 
Shatabdi train were therefore with drawn and services continued with 
conventional coaches. These problems have been carefully studied and 
necessary modifications have been carried out by experts from ALSTOM 
LHB in close coordination with Railway personnel to adapt these to Indian 
conditions. These modifications have been done by the supplier free of cost 
under the contractual obligations. The coaches are now ready for re-

2837. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether is is a fact that while the world average speed for 
passenger train movement is 300 kmph and freight trains is at 200 
kmph, such speeds in India are placed at 162 kmph and 75 kmph, 
respectively; 
(b) if so, the specific reasons identified for the low average speeds in 
India; and 
(c) the steps being taken to improve these speeds, including the details of 
phased measures contemplated in this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (c) Ministry of Railways does not have any 
official record about th e speed potential of frei ght and passenger trains 
operating on foreign railway systems. As per Jane's World Railways 1998-99 
publication, the fastest Highspeed Passenger Trains in the world are normally 
operating in the speed range of 275 to 300 kmph. The maximum speed 
recorded by high speed passenger trains in Japan is between 260—275 kmph. 
In the freight category, the Japanese Railways has Rolling stock capable of 
running at a speed of 130 kmph. 
Indian Railways has capability to run Passenger trains in the speed range of 
130—140 kmph and the goods trains in the speed range of 75—100 kmph. 
The reason for lower speed potential of passenger trains is that Indian 
Railways operate in a mixed traffi c environment, where slow moving 
passenger and goods trains and also fast moving Express trains run on the 
same track. In foreign countries such fast services are run on dedicated track 
with hightly sophisticated equipments. Investments in such services call for 
massive funds in dedicated infrastructure and corresponding maintenance 
facilities. Such ventures 
358 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
require very high volumes and paying capacity. 
Ministry of Railways is contemplating increasing the speed of good trains to 
100 kmph to reduce the speed differential between passener & freight trains.

2853. SHRIMATI SARLA MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of

for realization of charges for using rail lines/property;

(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (c) No, Sir. However, Railways generally

Bisley recently, have accused the Indian participants of stealing from the 
accommodation in which they were lodged;

(c) whether Government have inquired into the matter; 
(d) if so, what is the factual position; and

STATEMENT BY MINISTER AND DISCUSSION IN CONNECTION 
WITH 
TERRORIST ATTACK ON PARLIAMENT HOUSE ON THE 
13
TH
 DECEMBER, 2001 
THE LEADER OF THE HOU SE AND THE MINISTER OF 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir,... 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal) : Sir, we have to 
get copies of the statement. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, it is a legitimate requirement of 
copies in both Hindi and English. As I am making the statement, the 
statement is being replicated and will be here in the House available in 
sufficient copies very shortly. Su re. In the meantime, with your 
permission, Sir, on behalf of my senior colleague, the Home Minister, I 
would like to make the following statement in connection with the 
terrorist attack on Parliament House on 13* December, 2001. 
The ghastly attack on Parliament House on 13 th December, 
2001 has shocked the entire nation. The terrorist assault on the very 
bastion of our democracy was clearly aimed at wiping out the 
country's top political leadership. 
It is a tribute to our security personnel that they rose to the 
occasion and succeeded in averti ng what could have been a national 
catastrophe. In doing so, they made the supreme sacrifice for which 
the country would always remain indebted to them. It is now evident 
that the 
426 

[18 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
terrorists assault on the Parliament  House was executed jointly by 
Pak-based and supported terrorist outfits, namely, Laskar-e-Taiba and 
Jaish-e-Mohammad. These two organisations are known to derive 
their support and patronage from t he Pak I.S.I. The investigation so 
far carried out by the police shows that all the five terrorists, who 
formed a suicide squad, were Paki stani nationals. All of them were 
killed on the spot, and their Indian associates have since been 
nabbed and arrested. The investigation at this stage indicates that the 
five Pakistani terrorists entered the Parliament House Complex at. 
about 11.40 AM in an Ambassador Car, bearing registration No. DL-
3CJ-1527 and moved towards Building Gate No. 12 when it 
encountered the carcade of the Vice -President of India, which was 
parked at Gate No. 11. One of the members of the Parliament House 
Watch and Ward Staff, Shri Ja gdish Prasad Yadav, became 
suspicious about the identity of t he car, and immediately ran after it. 
The car was forced to turn backward, and in the process, it. hit the 
Vice-President's car. When chall enged by the security personnel 
present on the spot, all the five terrorists jumped out of the car and 
started firing indiscriminately. The Delhi Police personnel, attached 
with the Vice-President security, as also the personnel of the C.R.P.F. 
and the I.T.B.P. on duty immediately took their positions and returned 
the fire. It was at this point that another member of the Parliament 
House Watch and Ward staff, Shri Matbar Singh, sustained bullet 
injuries. He rushed inside Gate No. 11 and closed it. An alarm was 
raised and all the gates in the building were immediately closed. The 
terrorists ran towards Gate No. 12, and then to Gate No. 1 of the 
Parliament House Building. One terrorist was shot dead by the 
security forces at Gate No. 1, an d in the process, the explosives 
wrapped around his body exploded. The remaining four terrorists 
turned back and reached Gate No. 9 of the Building. Three of them 
were gunned down there. The fifth terrorist ran towards Gate No. 5 
where, he also was gunned down by the SPG personnel. During the 
exchange of fire, four Delhi Police personnel, namely, Shri Nanak 
Chand, Assistant Sub-Inspector, Shri Rampal, Assistant Sub-
Inspector.. Shri Om Prakash, Head Constable, and Shri Ghanshyam, 
Head Constable, attached with the Vice-President's security, lost their 
lives on the spot. The other three persons, who were also killed, were 
Smt. Kamlesh Kumari, a woman constable of C.R.P.F., Shri Jagdish 
Prasad Yadav, a security assistant of the Watch and Ward Staff of the 
Parliament House, who had rushed after the terrorists' car, and a 
civilian employee of the C.P.W.D., Shri Desh Raj. 
427 

RAJYA SABHA [18 December, 2001] 
Eighteen other persons were injured and they were immediately 
rushed to Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital for medical treatment. These 
included Shri Matbar Singh, Security Assistant, Watch & Ward Staff of the 
Parliament House, who later succumbed to his injuries. The scene of the 
crime was cordoned off and Investigation Teams, including Forensic 
Experts and Bomb Detection Squads, were pressed into service. A number 
of hand grenades were recovered from the site of the incident and defused. 
A large quantity of arms and ammunition, including explosives, was also 
recovered. 
The breakthrough in the investigation of the case was 
achieved with the arrest of Syed Abdul Rehman Geelani, a Lecturer in a 
local college, whose interrogation led to the identification of two other 
accomplices, Afzal and Shaukat Hussain Guru. The wife of the latter 
disclosed that her husband and Afzal had, in the afternoon of 13*" 
December, left for Srinagar. This information was immediately conveyed 
to the Jammu and Kashmir Police who apprehended both of them. A 
laptop computer and Rs. 10 lakhs in cash was recovered from them. 
They were later brought to Delhi by a Special Team deputed for the 
purpose by the Delhi Police. 
Interrogation of the accused persons has revealed that Afzal 
was the main coordinator, who was assigned the task by a Pakistani 
national, Gazi Baba of Jaish-e-Mohammed. Afzal had earlier been 
trained in a camp run by Pak-lSl at Muzaffarabad in Pak-occupied 
Kashmir. The hideouts for the five Pak terrorists were arranged by 
Shaukat Hussan Guru, two in Mukherjee Nagar and one in Timarpur 
area in North Delhi. During the subsequent raids, the Police recovered 
from two of these hideouts a large quantity of Ammonium Nitrate and 
other ingredients used in preparing Improvised Explosive Devices, a map 
of Delhi, a sheet of paper carrying a map of Chanakyapuri, drawn in hand, 
and three police uniforms. 
This incident once again established that terrorism in India is the 
handiwork of Pakistan-based terrorist outfits, known to derive their support 
and sustenance from Pak-ISI. The hijacking of IC-814 Flight to 
Kandahar, the terrorist intrusion into the Red Fort, and the attack on J & K 
Legislative Assembly Complex at Srinagar on 1* October, this year, were 
masterminded and executed by militant outfits, at the behest of the ISI. 
Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed, in particular, have been in 
the forefront in organising terrorist violence in the country. The 
Pakistan High Commissioner in India was summoned to the Ministry of 
External Affairs and 
428 

[18 December. 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
issued a verbal demarche, demanding that Islamabad take action 
against the two terrorist outfits involved in the afack on the Parliament 
House. 
Last week's attack on Parliament is undoubtedly the most 
audacious, and also the most alarming, act of terrorism in the nearly two-
decades-long history of Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in India. This 
time, the terrorists, and their mentors across the border, had the temerity to 
try to wipe out the entire political leadership of India, as represented in our 
multiparty Parliament. 
Naturally, it is time for all of us in this august House, and all of 
us in the country, to ponder why the terrorists and their backers tried to 
raise the stakes so high, particularly, at a time when Pakistan is claiming 
to be a part of the international coalition against terrorism. 
The only answer that satisfactorily addresses this query is that 
Pakistan-itself a product of the indefensible Two-Nation Theory; itself a 
theocratic State with an extremely tenuous tradition of democracy-is 
unable to reconcile itself with the r eality of secular, democratic, self-
confident and steadily progressing India, whose standing in the international 
community is getting inexorably higher, with the passage of time. 
The Prime Minister, in his address to the nation on 13th December, 
2001, has declared that the fight against terrorism had reached a decisive 
phase. The supreme sacrifice made by the security personnel, who 
lost their lives in this incident, will not be allowed to go in vain. Those 
behind the attack on Parliament House should know that the Indian 
people are united and determined to stamp out terrorism from the 
country.  Thank you. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Mr. Chairman, I thank the 
hon. Minister of External Affairs and the Leader of the House for the 
statement that he has made. Most of the facts stated by him in this 
statement have already appeared in the Press. Our party joins all our 
countrymen In condemning the dastardly terrorist attack on Parliament on 
13th December. Parliament is the heart and the nerve centre of our 
democracy and that is, probably, the reason why this terrorist gang tried to 
strike at the citadel of democracy, that is, our Parliament. 
429 

RAJYA SABHA [18 December. 2001]  
Sir, our party is one with the nation in its solemn resolve that we 
shall not make any compromises with these terrorist gangs. We shall pay 
whatever price is necessary to wipe out terrorism, and we are sure that our 
nation will prevail in this regard. 
Sir, on this occasion, our thoughts, our minds and our hearts go to 
those brave security personnel and members of the Watch and Ward 
Staff of our Parliament, who, in an act of supreme sacrifice, in an act of 
supreme devotion to their duty, laid down their lives to save the honour and 
dignity of this august House. Our sympathies go to the members of the 
bereaved families; to those who have suffered injuries, we wish them 
speedy recovery. 
Mr. Chairman, this is not an occasion to apportion blame or find 
fault with our system, w hether it is of intelligence or of security 
arrangements. Yet, it is a fact that  an attack on Parliament was quite 
anticipated. As early as on the 5th of this month, the hon. Home Minister, 
speaking at a meeting of the Feder ation of Indian Chambers of 
Commerce and Industry, had alluded to this threat to our Parliament. 
In fact, one day before this attack took place, i.e. on I2 m 
December, while speaking at Mumbai, the hon. Prime Minister himself 
had referred to the existence of this threat, such a threat to our Parliament. 
Subsequently, we have also learnt t hat the Maharashtra police, while 
interrogating a suspect Al-Qaeda member, Afroz in Mumbai informed the 
Central Government of the plans of this outfit to attack the Parliament. I 
have been told that the Maharashtra Government had informed the 
Central Government about what Afroz had told them. I have also been 
tdd that a member of the IB was also associated with the interrogation of 
Afroz.

to evolve a consensus. Of course, the Government has made a statement 
now; and we are getting an opportunity to discuss on this important issue. Sir, 
we do not deny the surprise element in su ch terrorist attacks.    We agree that 
determined terrorists can attack at any 
439 

RAJYA SABHA [18 December, 2001]  
time. But this attack of 13 th December was not a sudden affair. The Ministers, 
the leaders of all the political parti es belonging to the NDA have time and 
again been saying, "We are living with terrorists not only during the last few 
years, but for decades'. Some of them have even said, "We are living with 
terrorist attacks for centuries together". So. this is not a new phenomenon. The 
attack of October 1 on the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly was a pointer, 
again, the Home Minister made a revelation at the FICCI meeting that he had 
got direct evidence from various sources about a possible attack by terrorists 
on Indian Parliament. The Prime Minister expressed similar views at a meeting 
held in Mumbai. Despite all these, what prevented the Government from taking 
adequate measures? Of course, the security forces belonging to the CRPF, 
the ITBP, the SPG, the Delhi Police and the Watch & Ward Wing of the 
Parliament House, challenged the terrorists and killed them. Certainly, we all 
congratulate them for their valour. This shows that if proper arrangements had 
been made, we would have averted the attack. What prevented the 
Government from taking sufficient prot ective measures at the gate of the 
Parliament House? They had the evidence; many talks were going on, and 
earlier experience also showed that something could happen. The security 
forces challenged the terrorists inside the Parliament complex and killed them. 
So, if sufficient arrangements had made at the gate, they could have been 
stopped there itself. That is why I say t hat there was a security lapse on the 
part of the Government. There is a world of difference between the 
performance of the security staff and the security arrangements made by the 
Government. Of course, ou r security forces prov ed their efficiency. But, 
despite all the available information, the Government failed to make adequate 
arrangements to prevent the terrorists at  the gate. Sir. the question before us 
is, what should be the future course of action? What we want is not a knee-
jerk reaction. We need a well thought-out strategy to face the challenge of the 
terrorists. Sir, all those who planned and perpetrated the attack should be 
punished. And, we should also be able  to prevent the repetition of such 
incidents. How to achieve that? For achi eving this, the most important thing is 
that there should be unity inside t he country and outside the country. Of 
course, there is a growing awareness in the international community about 
such terrorists' attack. Collect all evidence; go before the international 
community and convince the international community. Go to the United 
Nations. We are not asking for their involvement. What we require is a broader 
unity among the international community to force Pakistan not to allow the 
terrorist forces 
440 

[18 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
from operating in their country. The Pres ident of Pakistan has said that if 
proper evidence is brought before him, he would take appropriate measures. 
What appropriate measures would he ta ke? Let us collect all the evidence; 
get the support of the international community and try to force Pakistan to 
take action. This is the best course of action in the pr esent situation. Of 
course, many statements were issued. W hat is the line of thinking of the 
United States of America on this issue?  What did the U.S. Secretary of State 
say? He is asking us to show some restraint. What is the attitude of other 
countries? What initiatives have been taken by the Government to rally the

making irresponsible statements. Sir,  the Government should take all 
appropriate measures for preventing the repetition of such incidents. 
Certainly, the entire count ry is one on the issue of meeting the challenge 
thrown by the terrorists. So, it is the responsibility of the Government to see 
that the whole country is united on this issue. It is the responsibility of the 
Government to see that the international community is also united on this 
issue. Sir, we don't agree, with the statements made by some of the hon. 
Members belonging to the major political  parties of the NDA, that we should 
attack the terrorist camps in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. That would only 
unleash a war between India and Pakistan. Both the countries are nuclear 
countries. Not only that, Sir; that will also divide the international community. 
What we require is, unity among the international community. Then only we 
would be able to force Pakistan to take measures against the perpetrators of 
this terrorist attack; then only we would be able to force Pakistan not to allow 
its territory to be used by these terro rists for cross-border terrorism. So, we 
should take such steps that would faci litate unity among the people and also 
among the international community.  With these words, I conclude. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir, for

last 20 years and for which a large number of 
442 

[18 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
people have sacrificed their lives -- in Jammu and Kashmir alone, more than

RAJYA SABHA [18 December, 2001]

444 

[18 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
information; and some of the information you can share with us at this critical

RAJYA SABHA [18 December, 2001]  
Again, Mr. Chairman, Sir, most respectfully, I would like to submit

The third question which, most legitimately, can be put is this. It is

[18 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA

nation in condemning this dastardly act, which took place on December 13, on

[18 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
Minister had been demanded,. Sir, when a similar incident took place in the

would  have become very  dangerous

RAJYA SABHA [18 December. 2001]  
throughout the globe. So, I request the hon. Foreign Minister to take diplomatic

SHRI C.P. TH.IRUNAVUKKARASU (Pondicherry): Thank you. Mr. Vice-
Chairman, for giving me an opportunity to speak on this subject. 
Sir, thirteen is a bad number for certain people; for certain people, 
it may be a good number. In the 11" Lok Sabha, our Prime Minister, Shri 
Vajpayee, ruled for thirteen days only, but he came back to power again in 
the 13th Lok Sabha. This incident also took place on the thirteenth. But. I 
am sure, our hon. Prime Minister will overcome this situation, with the 
support of all political parties. I recollect that just two days prior to the 
incident on 13th, pandemonium was prevailing in the House, as both sides 
were quarrelling over an issue. But, today, the only issue before the House 
is : Are we united together or not? The nation is witnessing it. We are not 
able to prove that we are united in order to prevent the terrorists from 
entering into our territory. The attack on the Parliament on i3m December 
was an attack on democracy; it was an attack on our freedom. Our 
security forces and personnel of the Watch & Ward have laid down their 
lives so that democracy can survive. 
The cowardly and dastardly attack was on the freedom of the 
country and democracy. Senseless elements, having no faith in democratic 
institutions, had carried out the attack.   But we are firm in our determination

DR. L.M. SINGHVI (Rajasthan): Madam, "may I first of all pay my 
tribute to those who fell victims to the dastardly attack on the Parliament 
House? They deserve our deepest grat itude and they deserve the greatest 
praise. They lived the lives of very brave persons and they died as very brave 
individuals. I think it is well to say that such dedicated persons who are deeply 
devoted to their duty, like the security staff and the Watch and Ward of 
Parliament, create that faith which is im portant. It was their faith in the nation 
and their sense of duty which inspired them to make the supreme sacrifice of 
their lives in a battle, in a war against terrorism. We can make no mistake that 
those martyrs died in our battle against terrorism in India. Terrorism has, in 
fact, engaged itself in many such skirmishes and battles; but, now, with their 
attack on Parliament House, they appear to have declared their war on India 
and Indian democracy. And this declaration of war on Indian democracy is 
something which all of us must fight together and with a total sense of 
solidarity. That is why I thought it was a welcome occasion to make a common 
cause, to make certain that we speak in unison, with our views orchestrated in 
solidarity, and we may then forge those strong ties in speaking politically 
amongst ourselves and to the world be more able and strong to fight the battle 
against terrorism. In these two decades, we have faced many battles against 
terrorism; in these battles, we have faced them, more or less, single-handed, 
as a nation. The nm September attack on the twin Towers, I had hoped, would 
make a difference, at least in terms of converts KJ India's war against terrorism 
into a global war against terrorism. That is what we understood the message 
of President Bush to be.   I hope that this attack on the Parliament of India will

DR. RAJA RAMANNA (Nominated): Mada m, first of all, I would like 
to express my condolences to the bereaved families of those persons who 
have actually saved us in many ways. While talking about this attack and the 
origin of this attack, I am taken back to the days before Partition when we 
were in college. At that time, one thing that worried us the most was the 'Quit 
India Movement'. But in the deep Sout h, there were groups of people who 
used to say that Partition of the count ry was only temporary and that they 
would come back and take power in India again. I think it is this kind of 
attitude that people still have in the ne ighbouring country which makes them 
believe that they can come back through terrorism and take back power 
again. It is not a trivial statement I am making. It is something which is deeply 
buried in the minds of the people who at  the time of Partition were a bit 
unhappy and felt that t he Partition was moth-eaten  and that the Partition 
programme had not been fulfilled and that they have to come back to take 
power again. This is my view. Otherwise, such intense use of weapons and 
planning that has been shown cannot be explained away easily. But my 
purpose of speaking today is not to ta lk about what has already happened but 
to know how we have to fa ce the future in  the months to come. I am sure, 
there will be attacks again. How do we prepare ourselves for that? We have to 
take a lesson from the war that has ta ken place in Afghanistan. The Talibans 
were defeated very easily. They coul d not have been defeated easily by the 
Northern Alliance but for the support of the American and the European 
forces. It means we tiave got to find out if a conflagration takes place, are we 
ready to win the war. What made t he Taliban collapse that way? It is 
essentially the automat ion, the air activity, the target-bombing of places, the 
large scale attacks, which frightenec the people. After all, the Afghans are not 
ordinary people. They are known for their great courage and great 
performance levels.    But the

make sure that we have pi lotless aircraft in case of  air attacks; I know, I am
